PREFACE. 


i 


THE present volume contains the extant Ex- 
chequer accounts ofthe first nine yearly audits of 
the reign of James Iv., namely, from 1488 to 1496 
inclusive, consisting of the burgh accounts of all 
these years, and the accounts of the Crown lands for 
the same years except 1493, also an account of the 
Comptroller of the Household, written on paper 
and in book form, two separate and not quite 
identical copies of which have been preserved, both 
in a rather mutilated condition. The place of 
audit was most frequently Edinburgh or Stirling, 
sometimes Linlithgow; and the time of meeting of 
the Exchequer was generally in June, the audit 
going on till August, An account of the bailies of 
Inverness for a disturbed period was rendered at 
that burgh in the month of November; and the 
account of the Comptroller was, agreeably to usual 
practice, audited at a separate diet held in January 
1492-3. | 

In this volume, as in the last,an Appendix is 
added with the Rentals of the Crown lands for its 
period and the continuation of the Index to the 


xxxvi PREFACE. 


Responde Books from 1492 to 1496. The years from 
1484 to 1491 are a blank in this Index, the Libri 
Responsionum for those years having probably been 
lost before it was made. 

The following remarks bear chiefly on the light 
thrown by these records of the general history of 
the time, including the closing scene of the reign of 
James III. 

The negotiations alluded to in the Preface to 
volume ninth, for the marriage of James n. with 
the widow of Edward tv., and of his sons with the 
daughters of Henry vir, seem to have been cut 
short by James stipulating for the surrender of 
Berwick as a condition. The émeute at Lauder 
had undoubtedly had the effect of rousing the King 
to a better sense of his regal duties, and leading 
him to turn his attention as he had never before 
done to the administration of justice and suppres- 
sion of crime. But the faction of the Earl of Angus, 
conscious that their past conduct was beyond for- 
giveness, saw danger in the strengthening of the 
royal authority, and, renewing their intrigues with 
England, set themselves to organise a fresh revolu- 
tionary movement. In May 1488 a safe conduct 
was granted by Henry vu. to the Bishops of 
Glasgow and Dunkeld, the Earl of Argyle, Lord 
Hailes, Lord Lyle, the Master of Darnley, and 
the Master of Hume, all of whom are known to 
have belonged to the faction hostile to the King.’ 


1 Rotuli Scotie, ii. 485. 
* 


PREFACE. xxxvii 


James Schaw of Sauchie, who had been Chamber- 
lain of Stirlingshire throughout most of the reign 
of James 1., and been made Keeper of Stirling 
Castle by that King,’ was ready at the call of these 
conspirators to betray the trust which had been 
reposed in him. Angus’ party gaining through 
him possession of the person of the Prince, now in 
his fifteenth year, inflamed his ambition with the 
prospect of a crown, and used every artifice to 
poison his mind against his father. It may be 
that their aim was to depose the King and confer 
the regency on the young Prince, rather than to 
adopt any measures directly affecting the King's 
life: but they were at least at all hazards resolved 
to make it impossible for James to reign. 

Next to Angus the most prominent in the ranks 
of the conspiraters were the Master of Hume, the 
head of the house of Hepburn, Lords Gray and 
Lyle, and John Lord Drummond, who had been re- 
cently made a Lord of Parliament. There was a 
special cause for the dissatisfaction of the Humes, 
James having some years previously annexed to 
the chapel royal founded by him in Stirling Castle 
the revenues of the priory of Coldingham, a 
religious establishment to which that family con- 
sidered that they had something like a patrimonial 
right. The annexation obtained the papal confir- 
mation in 1487: and an Act of the same year, 
which declared opposition to the King’s scheme to 


1 Page 3. 


xxxvili PREFACE. 


be treason, helped to kindle into a flame the 
smouldering torch of rebellion. The southern part 
of the kingdom having become a scene of revolt 
and violence, James by a sudden move made his 
way through Angus to Aberdeen, where he found: 
himself at the head of a large following.’ 
Returning southwards in May with a numerous 
retinue, including Athole, Huntly, Erroll, Crawford, 
Lindsay of the Byres, and Ruthven, he encountered 
the rebels at Blackness, where, after an indecisive 
skirmish, negotiations were opened, and articles of 
agreement entered into, which resulted in the dis- 
banding of the royal army, and a virtual triumph 
to the malcontents. In the brief interval before 
the final outbreak, James rewarded with lands and 
titles some of the most devoted of his followers, 
making the Earl of Crawford Duke of Montrose, 
and Lord Kilmaurs Earl of Glencairn. He bestowed 
the title of Duke of Ross on his second son, whom, 
rather than the misguided prince who now headed 
his enemies, he began to regard as his prospective 
successor. But no sooner had the King taken up 
his residence in Edinburgh Castle than the in- 
surgents were again in arms; and proceeding to 
Stirling with a hastily assembled force, he com- 
mitted his fortune to a battle on St Barnabas’ day 
(11th June) 1488, when, almost on the spot where

his recovery of the weapon and treasure, James 
Iv. bestowed on Simson for life those parts of the

youngistoun and Wattesmethistoun.?

But while devotedness to James 111. was generally 
construed as treason to James Iv., there were a few 
of the staunchest adherents of the late King in 
whose case it seems to have been assumed that the 
same conscientious principle of loyalty to their 
sovereign which had attached them to the father 
would keep them faithful to the son, The Duke of 
Montrose or Earl of Crawford had, even before the 
meeting of Parliament in October, a full remission 
under the Privy Seal. The same was extended to . 
the famous sea captain Sir Andrew Wood, notwith- 
standing the boldness of speech which he is said to 
have used to the Council immediately after Sauchie- 
burn. It was rightly presumed that his allegiance 
would be unhesitatingly transferred from his dead 
master to that master’s heir: and as early as 
the 27th July the party in power granted him a 
renewal of his feu-charter of Largo.*

those recorded as present had taken a more or less 
prominent part against the late King, including the 
Earls of Angus and Argyll, Lord Hailes, the Master 
of Hume, Lords Glammis, Lyle, Gray, and Drum-

Disaffection broke out before long in two dif- 
ferent quarters, It is with surprise that we find 
two adherents of the government to whom Parlia- 
ment had entrusted the preservation of peace in the 
west, Lord Lyle, the Justiciary, and the so-called 
Earl of Lennox, now Governor of Dumbarton Castle, 
organizing an insurrection in the district committed 
to their keeping, and holding out the fortress of 
Dumbarton against the Crown. They were in 
communication with another set of insurgents in 
the north, friends of James 111., among whom Lord 
Forbes made himself conspicuous by displaying the 
late King’s bloody shirt as the banner of revolt. 
A Parliament was assembled on 26th June 1489, 
when Lennox and his son and Lyle were forfeited ; 
and it was agreed that the King, at the head of his 
host, should pass at once to Crookston and Duchal, 
while Argyll would be sent to bombard Dumbarton. 
Duchal was reduced, and the artillery were on their 
way back hefore the end of July : and on the 4th of

to Denmark, to renew the existing commercial 
league with, that country. The former embassy 
had a safe conduct from the King of England on

for France? and returned in November following 
without having gone to Spain. We find Bothwell 
allowed the custom of 18 sacks of wool for his

The proceedings of the Parliament of February 
1491-2 testify to the continued existence of a 
wide-spread feeling against the party in power as 
being implicated in the late King’s death, an 
impression which they tried to combat by offering 
a reward of 100 marks worth of land to any one 
who should make known to the King who were the 
actual slayers of his father with their own hands, 
and declaring guilty concealment of this matter to 
be equivalent to treason.’

II. 


The lawless condition of the Highlands and 
Islands seems about this time to have forced itself 
on James's attention. Thirteen years had passed 
since the overgrown power of the Lord of the Isles 
had been abridged by his compulsory surrender 
to the Crown of the earldom of Ross and of Kin- 
tyre and Knapdale; but this necessary step had 
not been effective in establishing order and tran- 
quility either in north or in west. The chief 
disturber of the peace for some time was the same 
Angus Og who had been the masterspirit of the 
rebellion of 1462, and who, though but an illegiti- 
mate son of the Island potentate, had in 1476 been 
constituted heir to his title as a Lord of Parliament, 
and to his domains. The revolt of this Angus, 
and the measures taken to suppress it, are matters 
belonging to the reign of James 11. on the rather 
obscure chronology of which the Exchequer Rolls 
shed but a faint light. The culminating point of

PREFACE. Ixvii 


APPENDIX TO PREFACE. 


NOMES 
DEATH OF THE LAST EARL op DovaGras. 


The date of the death of James, ninth and last Earl of 
Douglas, has often been given as 15th April 1488. In 
noticing in the Preface to Volume Ninth (page lv) the 
mention in the English records of date 2nd February 
1486-7, of “ Anna que fuit uxor Jacobi Douglas comitis 
de Douglas,” the question was raised, but not answered 
whether these words should be taken as implying that the 
Earl was then dead. The inquiry seems to be answered 
in the negativein the present volume. Sir James Douglas, 
Knight, whom it is not easy to identify with any one 
but the ex-Earl, had, the Kinclevin account of 1489 
informs us, a pension of £200 granted him under the 
Great Seal of James IV. The grant is unrecorded in the 
Great Seal Register, but payments of a portion of it 
(namely £121, 6s. 8d.) which was allocated on the fermes ` 
of Kinclevin, etc., appear in the accounts of 1489, 1490, 
and 1491. In the Kinclevin account rendered July 1491 
(page 253) the accountant is credited with the whole 
£121, 6s. 8d. as paid “quondam Jacobo Dowglas, militi,” 
which is said to be in satisfaction of his debts, besides a 
balance of arrears paid to his factors. It therefore seems 
that the last Earl of Douglas died, not earlier, but later 
than the usually assigned date, namely, in 1491. But, if 
so, how are the words “que fuit uxor" to be explained ? 
If he actually became a monk at Lindores, he may per- 
haps have been required to renounce his wife: but it is 
also supposable that there may have been a divorce on 
some unknown ground.

! Jacobus Dei gracia rex Scotorum, omnibus probis hominibus tocius 
terre sue clericis et laicissalutem. Sciatis nos quandam cartam feodifirme 
factam et concessam per quondam nostrum bone memorie patrem, cujus 
anime propicietur Deus, dilecto nostro familiari servitori Andree Wod et 
heredibus suis de totis et integris terris de Largo cum pertinenciis jacent- 
ibus infra vicecomitatum nostrum de Fiffe, de mandato nostro visam, 
lectam, inspectam, et diligenter examinatam, sanam, integram, non rasam, 
non cancellatam nec in aliqua sui parte suspectam ad plenum intellexisse 
sub hac forma: Jacobus Dei gracia rex Scotorum, omnibus probis homin- 
ibus locuis terre sue clericis et laicis, salutem : Seiatis quod nos in tem- 
pore nostri parliamenti considerantes gratiata et fidelia servicia nobis per 
dilectum familiarem servitorem nostrum Andream Wod, commorantem in 
Leith, tam per terram quam per mare in pace et in guarra gratanter 
impensa in regno nostro et extra idem et signanter contra nostros inimicos 
Anglie, e& dampnum per ipsum Andream inde sustenta suam personam 
gravibus vite exponendo periculis, dedimus, concessimus et ad feodi- 
firmam dimisimus ac tenore presentis carte nostre damus, concedimus, et 
ad feodifirmam dimittimus ae confirmamus hereditarie dicto Andree Totas 
et integras terras nostras et vilam de Largo cum pertinenciis, jacentes 
infra vicecomitatum nostrum de Fiffe, quas nunc idem Andreas de nobis 
habet sibi et suis assignatis pro terminis novemdecim annorum, ut in 
nostris sub nostro secreto sigillo sibi inde prius confectis continetur: 
Tenendas et habendas totas et integras predictas terras et villam de Largo 
cum pertinenciis dicto Andree et heredibus suis de nobis et successoribus 
nostris in feodifirma et hereditarie imperpetuum per omnes rectas metas 
suas antiquas et divisas prout jacent in longitudine et latitudine in boscis 
et planis, moris, marresiis, viis, semitis, aquis, stagnis, rivolis, pratis, 
pasturis et pascuis, molendinis, multuris et eorum sequelis, aucupacion- 
ibus, venacionibus, piscacionibus, pratis et turbariis, carbonariis, lapicidiis, 
lapide et calce, fabrilibus, brasinis, bruariis et genestis, domibus, edificiis, 
mansionibus, hortis, pomeriis, columbis, columbariis, cuniculis, cunicu- 
lariis, cum curiis et earum exitibus,'heriyeldis, bludewitis et marchetis 
mulierum, ac cum omnibus et singulis libertalibus, commoditalibus, et 
asiamentis ac justis pertinenciis quibuseumque tam non nominatis quam 
nominatis ad dictas terras et willam de Largo cum pertinenciis spectan- 
tibus seu quovismodo juste spectare valentibus in futurum, libere, quiete, 
plenarie, integre, honorifice, bene et in pace sine revocacione aut contra- 
diecione nostri aut successorum nostrorum quovismodo in futurum:

quacunque aut contradiccione aliquali per nos aut successores nostros 
quovismodo inde facienda durantibus diebus vite eorundem. Quare vobis

et panni lanei dieti burgi qui pro tempore fueritis stricte precipimus et

viventi prefatam annuam pensionem quadraginta librarum de eisdem 
nostris custumis ad prefatos terminos prompte et integraliter persolvatis 
sine quocunque obstaculo aut impedimento, quam annuam pensionem in

librarum usualis monete regni Seocie de magnis custumis nostris dicti

tim persolvendam ad duos anni terminos usuales, Penthecostes videlicet 
et Sancti Martini in hieme, per equales porciones, introitus vero dicti 
domini Jacobi ad percepcionem et levacionem dicte annue pensionis 
vigenti librarum incipiens ad festum Sancti Martini datam proximo 
sequens, et deinde de termino in terminum per eum percipiendam et sibi 
annuatim ut premittitur persolvendam et deliberandam pro toto tempore 
vite sue semper et quousque per nos promotus fuerit ad beneficium vigenti 
librarum vel amplius : Tenendam et habendam dictam annuam pensionem 
vigenti librarum de dictis nostris custumis eidem domino Jacobo pro toto 
tempore vite sue semper et quousque promotus fuerit ut supra, libere, 
quiete, intigre, honorifice, bene, et in pace sine aliqua revocacione aut 
contradiecione quacunque. Quare vobis custumariis nostris dicte nostre 
magne custume burgi nostri predicti qui pro tempore fueritis stricte pre- 
cipimus et mandamus quatenus dicto domino Jacobo predictam annuam

allocare, ostensis semel coram eisdem auditoribus presentibus nostris 
literis et in libris sive rotulis compotorum registratis, ac eciam ostensis 
annuatim super compotum literis dicti domini Jacobi de recepto annue 
pensionis predicte. Datum sub magno sigillo nostro apud Edinburgh

de eodem, gardianum orientalium marchiarum seu limitum dieti nostri 
regni versus Angliam, pro spacio et terminis septem annorum datam 
presencium proxime et immediate sequencium, dando et concedendo 
eidem Alexandro, nostro gardiano, nostram plenariam potestatem et 
mandatum speciale curias gardiani dictarum marchiarum statuendi, 
inchoandi, affirmandi, et quociens opus fuerit continuandi, sectas vocandi 
et vocari faciendi, absentes amerciandi, transgressores et delinquentes 
secundum juris ordinem puniendi, amerciamenta et eschaetas levandi et 
recipiendi, et si necesse fuerit pro eisdem distringendi, attemptataque per 
nostros ligeos et subditos contra vim et effectum treugarum commissa 
reformandi, et consimilem reformacionem per gardianos alterius partis 
petendi et recipiendi, terminos debitos ad reformacionem hujusmodi 
faciendam statuendi et tenendi, et dictos nostros ligeos et subditos contra 
vim dictarum treugarum delinquentes, ut premittitur, puniendi, necnon 
locumtenentes et deputatos dictarum marchiarum ac ceteros officiarios in 
dicto officio necessarios pro quibus respondere voluerit, substituendi et 
deputandi, et generaliter omnia alia et singula faciendi, gerendi, et ex- 
cercendi que ad officium gardiani de jure seu consuetudine pertinent, 
pertinuerunt, seu quovismodo pertinere valent: Ratum et gratum habentes 
et habituri totum et quiequid dietus Alexander, noster gardianus, aut ejus 
locumtenentes, deputati, seu officiarii in dicto officio duxerit seu duxerint 
faciendi. Insuper dedimus et concessimus et per presentes damus et 
concedimus dicto Alexandro, nostro gardiano, pro sua administracione in 
dicto officio durantibus dictis septem annis, eadem et consimilia proficua, 
feoda, et debita sicut alii gardiani de nobis aut predecessoribus nostris aut 
quondam progenitore nostro bone memorie temporibus retroactis habu- 
erunt. Quare universis et singulis ligeis et subditis nostris quorum 
interest vel interesse poterit stricte precipimus et mandamus quatenus 
dicto Alexandro, nostro gardiano, suisque locumtenentibus, deputatis, et 
officiariis in omnibus et singulis dictum officium concernentibus duranti- 
bus dietis septem annis prompte. respondeant, pareant, et intendant, sub 
omni pena quam erga nostram regiam incurrere poterint majestatem.

foreste nostre nuncupatum Kirkhop, cum pertinenciis, jacentem in dicta

ac tenore presencium damus et concedimus dictis Alexandro et Alexandro

quibus respondere tenebuntur, durantibus terminis predictis, faciendi, 
deputandi, et substituendi, pro cujusquidem domus et fortilieii custodia

burgi receptis per compotantem ex tollerancia domini 
regis, quia prius habuit easdem in assedacione a domino 
rege, et tolleratur cum eisdem de terminis compoti, que 
firme extendunt se annuatim ad quinque libras. Summa 
hujus oneris patet. 

De quibus, allocate compotanti de summa oneracionis 
prediete ex eo quod tempore preterito trium annorum 
fuerunt guerre et perturbaciones in illis partibus, ita quod

interest vel interesse poterit stricte precipimus et mandamus ne quis dicto

James be the grace of God King of Scottis, to all and sindrie oure 
officiaris, liegis, and subditis quham it efferis quhais knawlage thir oure 
lettrez sal cum, greting. Wit ye us to have maid, constitut, and be thir 
oure lettrez makis, constitutis, and ordanis our traist and welebelovit 
cousingis and consalouris Coline erle of Ergyle, oure chancellar, Patrik 
lord Halis, maister of oure houshald, a venerable fadir fadir in God Johne 
prior of Sanctandros, o&re prive sele, Robert lord Lile, oure justice, 
Laurence lord Oliphant, Johne lord Drummond, sir Williame of Knollis, 
preceptour of Torfichin, oure thesaurar, maister Alexander Inglis, archdene 
of Sanctandros, our comptrollare, maister Williame Hepburne, vicar 
Linlithqw, clere of oure register, Archibald Edmonstoune of Duntreth, 
maister Richard Robisone, persone of Suthik, and Johne Hepburne of 
Rolandstoune, and thre of thame conjunctlie, oure said comptrollar 
beand ane of the thre, oure commissaris to the thingis within written, 
gevand and grantand to the saidis oure commissaris and to thre of thame 
conjunctlie, oure said comptrollare beand ane of the thre, oure full pouer 
and special mandiment to set all and sindre oure landis within oure 
realme that ar or beis lachfully fundin vacand for male, gressome, and 
dewtez for the termez of thre yeris or five yeris as thai think expedient, 
and to continew and prolong for the saidis termez or schortar the takkis 
of the personis that has ony now to ryn, courtis to hald, trespassouris to 
punys, amerciamentis, unlawis, and eschetis to raise, and thairfor gif ned 
be to distrenye and to inbring the samyn to oure use, chaumerlanis, 
custumaris, balyeis, and all uther officiaris necligent in their officis to 
remove, and utheris to chese and mak in thare stedis, and generalie all 
uthir and sindri thingis to do excerse and use that to the setting of the 
saidis landis, continewing and prolonging of takkis, removing and chesing 
of the said officiaris, and doing of al utber thingis belanging tharto of law 
or consuetud ar knawin to partene ; halding and for to hald ferme and 
stable all and quhatsumever thingis oure said commissaris or thre of 
thame conjunctlie, oure said comptrollare beand ane, in the thingis 
forsaidis in oure name richtwisly ledis to be done. Quharfor we charge 
straitlie and commandis yow all and sindri oure officiaris, liegis, and 
subditis forsaidis that ye and ilkane of yow redely intend, ansuer, and 
obey to the saidis oure commissaris and to thre of thaim conjunctly, oure 
said comptrollar beand ane of the thre as said is, in all and sindry the
